nghe.t: Part 1. You will hear a man telephoning an arts centre to ask about a pottery course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10.
Good morning, Hillside Arts Centre. Emma speaking.
Hi, good morning. I'm calling about the pottery course for beginners. I saw it on your website and I'd like to find out a bit more.
Of course. Can I take a few details first, so I can send you the information? What's your name?
It's Daniel Whitlock.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Sure. W, H, I, T, L, O, C, K.
W, H, I, T, L, O, C, K. Thank you. And a phone number, in case we need to contact you?
My mobile is 0117 496 0213.
0117 496 0213. Great. Now, the beginners' course runs on Saturdays, and there are two sessions — one in the morning, from ten to twelve, and one in the afternoon, from two to four.
The afternoon would be easier for me, to be honest.
Ah, I'm afraid the afternoon class is already full. We only take eight people in each group, and that one filled up last week. There are still three places in the morning session, though.
OK — the morning, then. Ten o'clock is fine.
Lovely. The course lasts eight weeks, and the first class is on the fourteenth of March. Not the seventh — we had to move it back a week because the studio is being repainted.
The fourteenth of March. Got it. And how much does it cost?
The full price is ninety-five pounds for the eight weeks. But if you book and pay before the end of this month, you get the early-booking price, which is eighty pounds.
Eighty pounds if I pay before the end of the month. That's good. Does that include the clay, or do I have to buy materials separately?
Everything is included — the clay, the glazes and the use of the kiln. The tools are provided too.
Do I need to buy an apron?
No, we lend aprons. But I'd wear an old shirt, because clay gets everywhere and it doesn't always wash out.
An old shirt — good tip. And what happens to the things I make?
You can keep up to three finished pieces. Anything beyond that we ask people to leave, simply because we don't have room to fire and store it all.
Three. That's fair. One more thing — where exactly are you? I've only been to Hillside once.
We're on Mill Lane. A lot of people think we're next to the station, but actually we're opposite the public library, about five minutes' walk from the station.
Opposite the library. Is there anywhere to park?
There's no parking at the centre, I'm afraid, so I'd advise against coming by car. The bus stops right outside, and there's a bike rack by the entrance.
I'll probably cycle, then. So what do I do next?
I'll email you a booking form this afternoon. Fill it in, send it back with the payment, and you're all set.
Perfect. Thanks very much, Emma.
You're welcome. See you in March, Daniel.

nghe.t: Part 2. You will hear the volunteer coordinator of a city farm talking to a group of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
Hello everyone, and welcome to Greenacre City Farm. My name's Tom and I'm the volunteer coordinator. Before we go outside, let me tell you a bit about the farm and how things work here.

People often assume the farm was set up by the council, because the council owns the land. In fact, it was started in 1986 by a group of parents from the local primary school, who wanted somewhere their children could see real animals. The council didn't get involved until much later, and the homelessness charity that uses our kitchen only arrived a couple of years ago.

What are we for today? Well, we do sell eggs and vegetables at the gate, but that brings in very little money, and we're not here to breed rare animals, although we do have two rare breeds of pig. The heart of what we do is education: we want every child in this part of the city to understand where their food comes from, and about nine thousand schoolchildren visit us each year.

A few rules for volunteers. We're flexible about hours — some people come for a couple of hours a week, others for a whole day; it's up to you. We lend out boots and waterproofs, so there's no need to buy any. But one thing isn't optional: before you work with any of the animals, you have to attend a two-hour training session, which we run on the first Tuesday of every month. That's for your safety and theirs.

And some news. We've had a café for several years now, and the second entrance on Park Road has been open since last spring. What's new this year is that from June to August we'll be staying open until eight in the evening, so we'll need volunteers for those extra hours too.
Right — now have a look at the plan of the farm. We're standing at the main gate, at the bottom of the plan.
As you come through the gate, the first building on your right is the volunteers' room. That's where you sign in, leave your bag and make a cup of tea.
Directly opposite it, on the left of the gate, is the tool store. Everything you need is in there — just remember to sign tools out and back in.
Now follow the main path up through the farm. Halfway along, on your left, between the path and the orchard, you'll find the vegetable garden. That's where most new volunteers start.
On the other side of the path, on your right, just before you reach the goat field, there's the pond. Please keep children on the path there — the edge is muddy.
The chickens used to live next to the barn, but we moved them last year. Their house is now in the far corner on the left, behind the orchard, where there's more shade.

At the top of the path is the barn, our biggest building. The café is in the wing attached to the right-hand side of the barn — not the small hut in the top right corner; that's where we store the animal feed.
One last thing: on the left of the path, just before the barn, are the beehives. Please don't go near them unless you're with the beekeeper.
OK, grab a pair of boots and let's go and meet the goats.

nghe.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Lena and Ravi, discussing their research project with their tutor, Dr Alvarez. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30.
So, Lena, Ravi — you've done your first two days of observation at the city museum. How did it go?

Mixed, I'd say. The staff were really helpful — they let us stand wherever we wanted. But we had a problem we hadn't expected: visitors kept noticing us. One man actually came over and asked what we were writing down.
And once people know they're being watched, they behave differently. A couple of them stood in front of a painting for ages, I think just to look serious.
That's a classic problem with observation. What else?

Our recording sheet. We designed it with twelve columns — time of arrival, time leaving, number in the group, whether they read the label, and so on. It was far too complicated. By the time I'd filled in one row, the person had moved on to the next room.

We were worried the museum might close early on the Sunday, because of a private event, but in the end it stayed open as normal. And there was no shortage of visitors — on the Saturday there were so many that we lost track of the people we were following.
OK. So let's think about improvements. Ravi, you said timing was difficult?
Yes. I was using my watch and writing times down by hand. I'd like to use a timer app on my phone instead — you just tap when someone arrives and tap again when they leave, and it records everything.
Good. Lena?
I think we should add a short questionnaire — just three questions, handed out at the exit. Otherwise we only know what people did, not why they did it.

That's sensible, as long as it's genuinely short. I'd add two things myself. First, you've only observed at weekends. You need to go back at different times of the week, because weekday visitors — retired people, school groups — behave quite differently.
That's true. We'd assumed Saturday was typical.

And second, there's a published study from a museum in Melbourne that measured exactly what you're measuring. Compare your results with theirs — it'll give you something to discuss in your conclusion.
We'll find it. So, what's the plan from here?
First, we rewrite the recording sheet so it fits on one page, with no more than five columns.
Then we go back and collect data on a weekday morning, when it's quiet, so we can actually follow people.
And enter everything into a spreadsheet as you go, not at the end. You'll thank yourselves later.
Right. And then we produce the draft. We're presenting a poster rather than a talk, so we'll send you a draft of the poster by the twentieth.
Perfect. Any questions? No? Then I'll see you both in two weeks.

nghe.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about Roman concrete. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Good afternoon. Last week we looked at steel. Today I want to turn to a material that is far older and, in one respect, far more impressive: Roman concrete.

Consider the evidence. Along the coast of Italy there are harbour walls, built by Roman engineers, whose concrete has survived roughly two thousand years of pounding by the sea — and in many places it is in better condition today than when it was poured. In Rome itself stands the Pantheon, completed in the second century, whose roof is still the largest dome in the world made of unreinforced concrete. Modern concrete, by contrast, typically begins to crack within a few decades, and a structure exposed to seawater may need major repair long before its designers intended.

So what did the Romans know that we have forgotten? The first part of the answer has been understood for a long time. Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash from the region around Naples — a material we still call pozzolana, after the town of Pozzuoli. When the ash reacts with lime and water, it forms a dense mineral network that binds the mixture together. In harbour structures something even more remarkable happens: seawater seeps into the concrete, reacts with the ash, and grows new crystals inside it, so the material actually becomes stronger over time rather than weaker.

But the ash alone does not explain everything, and here we come to a discovery made only a few years ago. If you look closely at a piece of Roman concrete, you will see small white lumps scattered through it, each a few millimetres across. These are fragments of lime, and they are known as lime clasts. For generations, scholars assumed they were simply a sign of poor mixing — evidence that Roman workers had been careless. A team of materials scientists decided to test that assumption, and they found that the clasts had a very specific internal structure, one that could only have formed at high temperature. That led them to a new reading of the Roman recipe.

Let me lay out the comparison, because it matters. In modern concrete, the binding agent is Portland cement, which is made by heating limestone and clay in a kiln and grinding the result into powder, and the whole mixture is prepared at room temperature. For a long time, scholars assumed that the Romans worked in a similar way, using lime that had already been slaked — that is, combined with water — before it went into the mix. The new evidence suggests they did something different. They added their lime as quicklime, which had not been slaked, and the reaction with water generated intense heat as the concrete was mixed. The researchers call this hot mixing. The heat speeds up the chemistry, and it leaves those lime clasts behind — not as a mistake, but as a built-in feature.

Why does that matter? Because of what happens when the concrete cracks, and all concrete cracks eventually. In a modern structure, a small crack grows, water gets in, and eventually it reaches the steel reinforcement inside, which rusts, expands and splits the concrete from within. In the Roman material, when a crack runs through one of those lime clasts, water dissolves the lime, carries it along the crack, and there it reacts and hardens again as calcium carbonate — effectively sealing the crack before it can spread. The concrete heals itself.

The researchers tested this directly. They made two batches of concrete, one using the Roman hot-mixing method and one using a conventional process, cracked both, and ran water through them. Within two weeks, the Roman-style samples had sealed completely. The conventional ones never did.

Now, I want to be careful about the lesson here. Nobody is suggesting we return to building with Roman recipes; modern concrete is stronger under load and can be poured far faster. A typical modern structure is designed to last around fifty years, and for many purposes that is perfectly acceptable. But concrete production is responsible for a large share of global carbon emissions, and a material that repairs its own cracks could last far longer and need far less replacement. Several companies are now trying to produce self-healing concrete based on the Roman approach. Whether it can be made at scale, and at a price the industry will pay, is the question we will take up next week.

READING PASSAGE 1
A SHORT HISTORY OF THE PENCIL
How a lump of black rock found under a fallen tree became the most common writing tool on Earth

Few objects are as familiar, or as little noticed, as the pencil. It costs almost nothing, needs no power and works upside down, under water and in freezing cold, which is why astronauts, divers and mountaineers still carry one. Yet the pencil in your drawer is the product of more than four centuries of trial, error and competition between nations.
The story begins in the north of England in the 1560s. According to local tradition, a violent storm uprooted trees on a hillside near the village of Borrowdale, and underneath them farmers found a deposit of a soft, black mineral. They quickly discovered that it left a dark mark on anything it touched and began using it to label their sheep. The material was graphite, although at the time people believed it was a form of lead, which is why we still speak of pencil "lead" today. The Borrowdale deposit was unusually pure, and for about two hundred years it was the only large source of solid graphite in the world. It became so valuable that the mine was guarded, and smuggling graphite out of the area was made a serious crime.
Early pencils were simply sticks of graphite wrapped in string or sheepskin to keep the user's fingers clean. Later, craftsmen in Italy and Germany learned to cut the mineral into thin strips and glue them between two pieces of wood — the basic design we recognise today. However, pure graphite was expensive and increasingly scarce, and attempts to mix the powder with glue or wax produced pencils that were either too soft or too crumbly to be useful.
The breakthrough came in France in 1795. Cut off from English supplies by war, the government asked an engineer and painter named Nicolas-Jacques Conté to find a substitute. Conté mixed powdered graphite with fine clay, pressed the mixture into rods and baked them in a kiln. His method had two great advantages. It used far less graphite, so poorer-quality deposits could be used, and by varying the amount of clay he could control how hard or soft the pencil was. More clay produced a harder, lighter line; more graphite a softer, darker one. The grading system still printed on pencils — from 9H, the hardest, to 9B, the softest, with HB in the middle — is a direct descendant of Conté's experiments.
Two later additions completed the modern pencil. In 1858 an American stationer, Hymen Lipman, was granted a patent for a pencil with a small rubber eraser fixed into one end. The idea proved enormously popular, although the patent was later cancelled by a court, which ruled that joining two existing products did not count as a new invention. The second addition was colour. In 1889 an Austrian firm displayed a luxury pencil painted bright yellow at the Paris World Fair. At the time the finest graphite came from China, where yellow was associated with royalty, and the company chose the colour to suggest quality. Rival manufacturers copied it, and in the United States yellow remains the standard colour for a pencil more than a century later.
Despite the arrival of the ballpoint pen in the 1940s and the computer keyboard a few decades later, the pencil has not disappeared. Around fourteen billion are still produced every year, most of them from cedar wood, which is soft enough to sharpen easily but strong enough not to split. Teachers value pencils because mistakes can be removed; artists and architects value the range of tones a single pencil can produce; and examination boards in many countries still insist on them, because the machines that mark answer sheets read graphite more reliably than ink. For an object that began as a way of marking sheep, it has had a remarkable career.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 2
THE RETURN OF THE NIGHT TRAIN
Written off as a relic twenty years ago, the European sleeper train is filling up again

A  For much of the twentieth century, the sleeper train was the natural way to travel long distances across Europe. Passengers boarded in the evening, ate in the dining car, slept in a narrow bunk and woke the next morning in another country. By the 1990s, however, the network was shrinking fast. Budget airlines could carry a passenger from Berlin to Rome for the price of a restaurant meal, and new high-speed day trains made many overnight journeys unnecessary. A trip that had once taken a whole night could now be completed in four or five hours, with a meal and a film thrown in. Railway companies, which found the ageing sleeper carriages expensive to maintain and difficult to fill, withdrew one route after another. In 2016 Germany's national operator closed its entire night-train business, and many observers assumed that the sleeper had reached the end of the line.
B  Yet within a few years the trend had reversed. The Austrian state railway, which had taken over several of the abandoned German routes, found that demand was far stronger than it had expected, and it began ordering new carriages. Its managers had expected the routes to lose money for years; instead, several were profitable within eighteen months. Private operators appeared in Sweden, the Netherlands and France, and by the early 2020s new or restored overnight services connected Vienna with Paris, Stockholm with Hamburg and Brussels with Berlin. Some routes sold out within hours of tickets going on sale. The night train, dismissed as a relic, had become fashionable.
C  The most obvious explanation is concern about climate change. A passenger travelling by train is responsible for a small fraction of the carbon emissions of the same journey by air — according to several estimates, less than one tenth. In Sweden the word "flygskam", or flight shame, entered everyday use to describe the embarrassment some people feel about flying for short trips, and its counterpart "tågskryt", meaning train pride, followed close behind. Surveys in several countries show that younger travellers in particular are willing to spend more time, and sometimes more money, in exchange for a lower-carbon route.
D  Environmental guilt alone, however, does not fill a train. Operators have also recognised that the sleeper competes not with a flight but with a flight plus a hotel. A traveller who leaves Paris at nine in the evening and arrives in Vienna at ten the next morning has saved the cost of a night's accommodation and lost no working time at all. For business travellers this calculation is attractive, and for tourists the journey itself becomes part of the holiday. Modern carriages reflect this shift: the newest designs offer private compartments with their own showers, individual sleeping pods for solo travellers, and breakfast delivered to the door. Some operators have gone further, offering cinema cars, bars with live music and family compartments that convert into playrooms during the evening. The aim is to make the hours on board feel like a hotel stay rather than a form of transport.
E  Running an overnight service is nevertheless far harder than it looks. A sleeper carriage carries perhaps a third as many passengers as a day coach of the same length, and it earns money only once a day, whereas a high-speed train can make several return journeys. Track access charges, which operators pay to use the rails, are calculated per kilometre and fall heavily on long-distance routes. A night train from Vienna to Brussels, for example, covers more than a thousand kilometres, and the fee for every one of them must be recovered from a few hundred sleeping passengers. Perhaps the greatest obstacle is the border. Each country has its own signalling systems, safety rules and electrical standards, so a train crossing three frontiers may need three locomotives and three sets of paperwork. One operator estimated that gaining approval to run a new international route took longer than building the carriages for it.
F  Governments have started to respond. The European Union has named rail travel a priority in its plans to cut transport emissions, and several national governments now offer direct subsidies to night-train operators or have promised to reduce access charges. Austria and France have each committed money to new rolling stock, and Sweden has paid an operator to run a service to Hamburg that would otherwise not exist. Progress on harmonising technical standards is slow but steady, and a new generation of locomotives able to run under several different electrical systems is removing one of the oldest barriers. Whether the sleeper can become more than a niche remains uncertain; it will never carry the numbers that budget airlines do. But for a growing minority of travellers, going to sleep in one city and waking up in another has once again become the most civilised way to cross a continent.

A  For much of the twentieth century, the sleeper train was the natural way to travel long distances across Europe. Passengers boarded in the evening, ate in the dining car, slept in a narrow bunk and woke the next morning in another country. By the 1990s, however, the network was shrinking fast. Budget airlines could carry a passenger from Berlin to Rome for the price of a restaurant meal, and new high-speed day trains made many overnight journeys unnecessary. A trip that had once taken a whole night could now be completed in four or five hours, with a meal and a film thrown in. Railway companies, which found the ageing sleeper carriages expensive to maintain and difficult to fill, withdrew one route after another. In 2016 Germany's national operator closed its entire night-train business, and many observers assumed that the sleeper had reached the end of the line.
B  Yet within a few years the trend had reversed. The Austrian state railway, which had taken over several of the abandoned German routes, found that demand was far stronger than it had expected, and it began ordering new carriages. Its managers had expected the routes to lose money for years; instead, several were profitable within eighteen months. Private operators appeared in Sweden, the Netherlands and France, and by the early 2020s new or restored overnight services connected Vienna with Paris, Stockholm with Hamburg and Brussels with Berlin. Some routes sold out within hours of tickets going on sale. The night train, dismissed as a relic, had become fashionable.

Surveys in several countries show that younger travellers in particular are willing to spend more time, and sometimes more money, in exchange for a lower-carbon route.

Some operators have gone further, offering cinema cars, bars with live music and family compartments that convert into playrooms during the evening. A night train from Vienna to Brussels, for example, covers more than a thousand kilometres, and the fee for every one of them must be recovered from a few hundred sleeping passengers. Perhaps the greatest obstacle is the border. Each country has its own signalling systems, safety rules and electrical standards, so a train crossing three frontiers may need three locomotives and three sets of paperwork. One operator estimated that gaining approval to run a new international route took longer than building the carriages for it.
F  Governments have started to respond. The European Union has named rail travel a priority in its plans to cut transport emissions, and several national governments now offer direct subsidies to night-train operators or have promised to reduce access charges. Austria and France have each committed money to new rolling stock, and Sweden has paid an operator to run a service to Hamburg that would otherwise not exist. nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 3
IS HANDWRITING WORTH SAVING?
A writer weighs the evidence for keeping the pen in the classroom

In 2014, Finland announced that its schools would no longer be required to teach joined-up handwriting, and the news travelled around the world with the speed usually reserved for celebrity scandal. Some commentators mourned the death of a civilised skill; others welcomed the end of a pointless ritual. Both reactions, I think, missed the point. The question is not whether handwriting is beautiful or traditional — it is whether it still does anything that typing cannot. Having spent two years reading the research and watching classrooms, I have come to believe that it does, though not for the reasons its defenders usually give.
The sentimental case is the weakest. Letters written by hand are said to carry a warmth that an email lacks; signatures express personality; a nation that cannot read its own old documents has lost touch with its past. There is something in each of these claims, but none of them justifies the hundreds of hours that schools devote to the subject. People managed perfectly well to express affection before literacy was widespread, and the number of adults who read eighteenth-century manuscripts for pleasure has always been tiny. Nor is it obvious that children who learn joined-up writing become more thoughtful correspondents; the warmest letters I have ever received were typed. If nostalgia were the only argument, the keyboard would deserve to win.
The practical case is stronger, and it rests on how writing by hand affects the brain. When a child forms a letter with a pencil, several things happen at once: the hand follows a shape, the eye checks the result, and the mind holds the sound the letter represents. Brain-imaging studies of young children show that this combination activates reading networks far more strongly than pressing a key does, and children who learn letters by writing them tend to recognise them faster than those who learn by typing. The advantage appears to persist: in one classroom study, children who had practised letters by hand in their first year were still ahead in reading twelve months later. The movement, it seems, is not a detour on the way to literacy but part of the road.
The effect does not stop in early childhood. A series of experiments with university students compared those who took lecture notes by hand with those who typed. The typists recorded more words — in some cases almost twice as many — yet when tested a week later, the handwriters remembered the ideas better. The likely explanation is uncomfortable for anyone who prizes efficiency: because writing by hand is slow, students cannot copy everything, so they are forced to decide what matters and to rephrase it in their own words. The typists, able to keep up with the lecturer, became transcribers rather than thinkers. Slowness, in other words, was doing useful work.
Sceptics raise two objections, and they deserve answers. The first is that these findings reflect habit rather than anything fundamental: a generation that grows up typing may learn to summarise on a keyboard just as well. This is possible, but so far the evidence does not support it; later studies that trained students to take fewer, more selective typed notes found that most slipped back into transcribing within minutes. The second objection is about time. Every hour spent perfecting the shape of a lower-case g, the argument runs, is an hour not spent on reading, mathematics or learning to code. Here I have more sympathy. Much of what passes for handwriting instruction is in fact instruction in neatness, and neatness has little to do with learning. A child who can write quickly and read back what she has written has the skill; whether her letters slope at the correct angle is a matter for calligraphers.
This points to a sensible middle course. Schools should teach children to write by hand fluently and legibly, because the act of forming letters supports reading and because note-taking by hand supports thinking. They should stop, however, treating elegant joined-up script as a goal in itself, and they should stop penalising children whose writing is untidy but clear. Nor should the keyboard be treated as an enemy. For a child with a physical difficulty that makes writing painful, or for an adult drafting a long report, typing is simply the better tool, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. What matters is that children leave school able to do both, and able to choose between them with some sense of when each is appropriate.
There is a final reason to hesitate before abandoning the pen, and it is the one I find hardest to measure and most difficult to dismiss. A handwritten page is a record of a process. Crossings-out, arrows and notes in the margin show how a thought developed, in a way that a clean typed document, with every revision silently erased, cannot. Writers, scientists and designers often say that they think on paper and then record on screen. The novelist who drafts in a notebook and the engineer who sketches before opening a design program are describing the same instinct. Whether this is a genuine cognitive advantage or merely a habit of the current generation, I cannot say. But a society that stopped teaching handwriting would be running an experiment on its children whose results would not be known for decades. Finland, incidentally, did not abolish handwriting at all; it dropped the requirement to teach one particular joined-up style while keeping printed letters. The reports of the pen's death, it turned out, were greatly exaggerated.
